blocks.text: How much damage swarms of locusts inflict on the regions of Syria and Egypt will be better understood from what the writers both of histories and of travels report to us. GREGORIUS BARHEBRAEUS, also called ABULPHARAGIUS, in his Chronicle, written in Syriac, copied by Bruns from a Bodleian manuscript and edited by Kirsch, p. 134: ܒܫܢܬ ܐܨܗ ܕܝ̈ܘܢܝܐ ܐܬܐ ܩܡܨܐ ܦܪܚܐ ܘܚܒܠ ܙܪ̈ܥܐ ܘܐܪܡܝ ܙܪܥܐ ܘܢܦܩ. ܘܡܣܒܟ ܗܘܐ ܘܣܠܩ ܒܫܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܐܣ̈ܐ. ܘܥܐܠ ܡܢ ܟܘ̈ܐ ܘܬܪ̈ܥܐ ܠܒ̈ܬܐ. ܘܐܬܡܠܝܘ ܡܢܗ ܐܦ ܓܪ̈ܒܐ ܕܡ̈ܝܐ ܘܬܫܘܝ̈ܬܐ ܘܦܬܘܪ̈ܐ ܘܠܓ̈ܐ. ܘܟܕ ܡܢ ܦܢܝܬ ܬܝܡܢܐ ܥܐܠ ܗܘܐ ܠܒܝܬܐ ܡܢ ܓܒܐ ܓܪܒܝܝܐ ܢܦܩ ܗܘܐ. ܘܐܟܠ ܥܡ ܥܣܒܐ ܘܐܝܠ̈ܢܐ. ܐܦ ܡܐ̈ܢܐ ܕܥܡܪܐ ܘܢܚ̈ܬܐ ܕܒ̈ܢܝܢܫܐ. ܘܟܕ ܓܡܪ ܠܟܠܗ ܦܢܝܬܐ ܕܐܘܪܗܝ ܘܣܪܘܓ ܥܒܪ ܠܡܥܪܒܐ. In the year of the Greeks 1095 (which was 784 after Christ) flying locusts burst in, spoiled the crops and laid eggs; and those hatched from them, after they had grown wings, climbed the walls and partitions, and entered the houses through the windows and doors [cf. Exod. X, 6. ומלאו בתיך ובתי כל עבדיך ובתי כל מצרים, They shall fill (the locusts) your houses, and those of your courtiers and of your subjects]. The water jars, the floors, the tables and the dishes were filled with them. After they had entered the houses from the southern side, they went out on the northern side, having consumed the plants, the trees, even the woollen garments and the clothing of men. When the whole region of Edessa and Sarug had been laid waste, they passed on towards the west. And the continuator of Barhebraeus, in dem Neuen Repertorio für bibl. und morgenl. Literat. edited by Paulus, vol. 1, p. 67 f. [the Syriac, 10 lines, not transcribed here]: In the year 1774 (1463 after Christ) many locusts came from the east, and wingless ones at that [so, it seems, the words ܘܕܒܒܐ ܐܝܬܝܗܘܢ ܗܘܐ should be rendered, which Bruns translated: and flies burst in. But ܕܒܒܐ here undoubtedly agrees in meaning with the Arabic دُبَّاءٌ [dubbāʾ], a locust not yet winged]. They came as far as Egypt, ate the crops, vineyards, fruits, trees, even the grass, and left nothing green on the face of the earth. The vineyards, fruits and trees failed, gnawed bare and devoured by the locusts. LEO AFRICANUS in the Descript. Africae [III, 284] book 2, ch. 11, p. 77, Zurich edition 1559: When I was staying among them (the people of Tagtessa), a great multitude of locusts had invaded that region; I would dare to affirm that they had grown so large that they far exceeded the ears of grain, which had then reached ripeness, so that the very surface of the ground was completely covered with locusts. [Cf. Exod. X, 15. ויכס את עין כל הארץ ותחשך הארץ They covered the whole surface of the earth and darkened it.] And this was in the year 919, which was 1510 of Christ. The same Leo, book 9, ch. 61, p. 512: In Africa locusts are generally seen in such numbers that in flight they cover the rays of the sun like a cloud. They eat the very trees together with their leaves and fruit. When about to depart they leave eggs, from which others spring up (although these do not fly), and wherever they are met with they eat everything down to the bark of the trees, and leave behind a great dearth of grain, especially in Mauritania. LE BRUN, Voyages au Levant p. 252, mentions a swarm of locusts that had consumed everything green within the space of two hours, and the places in Cyprus through which these insects had passed were as though laid waste by fire. Russell relates the same in the Natural History of Aleppo p. 62 (Of the noxious kind may well be reckoned the locust, which sometimes arrive in such incredible multitudes, that it would appear fabulous to relate, destroying the whole of the verdure where-ever they pass). Whoever wants more should consult OEDMANN in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 95 ff., and our Scholia on Exod. X, 14. p. 450 ff., second edition.
In Egypt barley ripens in the month of February; wheat lasts until the end of March, says Forsskål in the Prolegomenn. ad Flor. Aegypt. p. 43.
Compare the passage of Barhebraeus quoted above, note 1.
